question: Which Australian animal leaves cube-shaped droppings, stacked on rocks and logs to mark its territory?
source_excerpt: Wombats deposit droppings in prominent spots instead of hiding them, a territory-marking habit that has developed over generations.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone assumes droppings are round or log-shaped because nature doesn't make cubes. One animal does it anyway, and the flat sides stop the droppings rolling away.
extra.verification_notes: Wombats are the only animal known to produce cube-shaped droppings, and they place them on rocks and logs to mark territory (https://bgr.com/science/wombat-poop-cubes-study-research-nature/).

explanation: The cubes form inside the wombat's gut, where the intestinal wall stretches unevenly, and the flat sides keep the droppings from rolling off the rocks it uses as signposts.

question: Apart from apes and monkeys, one animal has fingerprints so similar to ours that experts struggle to tell them apart, even under a microscope. It lives on eucalyptus leaves. Which animal is it?
source_excerpt: not even careful analysis under a microscope could help distinguish the loopy, whirling ridges on koalas' fingers from our own.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume fingerprints are a human or at least primate trait. A distant marsupial evolved almost identical ones, and the eucalyptus clue lets them reason their way to it.
extra.verification_notes: Henneberg's research shows koala fingerprints are nearly indistinguishable from human ones even under a microscope, and koalas eat eucalyptus leaves (https://pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/koala-fingerprints/).

explanation: Koalas evolved fingerprints completely independently of us, most likely to grip branches and handle leaves, and they're so close to human prints that people joke they could confuse a crime scene.

question: One tiny sea creature can, when injured or starving, turn itself back into its baby form and start its whole life over again, potentially forever. What kind of animal is it?
source_excerpt: can revert to its sexually immature, colonial stage ... Theoretically, this process can repeat indefinitely, rendering it biologically immortal

extra.why_interesting: Every living thing is supposed to age in one direction. This creature runs its life backwards and starts again, and the players can reach the answer by thinking about which simple sea creatures change form during their lives.
extra.verification_notes: Turritopsis dohrnii, the 'immortal jellyfish', can revert from medusa to polyp under stress or injury, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turritopsis_dohrnii).

explanation: The so-called immortal jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii, can shrink back into a young polyp and grow up all over again, so in theory it never has to die of old age.

question: An octopus breaks one of nature's most basic rules: its blood isn't red. It carries oxygen using copper instead of iron. So what colour is octopus blood?
source_excerpt: Octopuses survive sub-zero temps thanks to specialized blue blood (hemocyanin, a copper-based oxygen carrier)

extra.why_interesting: Everyone assumes blood is red. But red only comes from iron. Players who picture old copper roofs or the green-blue Statue of Liberty can work out the answer, and then get the bonus surprise of three hearts.
extra.verification_notes: Octopus blood is blue because the copper-based hemocyanin turns blue when oxygenated; sources such as Scientific American and NBC News agree and nothing newer contradicts it.

explanation: Copper-based haemocyanin turns blue when it picks up oxygen, the same way copper roofs turn blue-green. Because this blood carries oxygen less efficiently, the octopus needs three hearts to pump it.
